content.evaluation:
Kanbur, Wu, and Duan offer a credible reason to investigate a thermal coupling, but do not establish their stronger claims about economic feasibility or an optimal design. Published in the International Journal of Energy Research in 2020, the paper addresses engineers accustomed to evaluating proposed systems through thermodynamic balances, component costing, and numerical optimization. Its purpose is both constructive and persuasive: introduce a new use for immersion-cooling waste heat, then show that the integration deserves practical development. The strongest conclusion is that a carefully bounded demonstration is worth investigating. The abstract's assertion of feasibility for real applications outruns the evidence.

The argument begins with data centers' cooling burden, moves through heat-recovery precedents, and identifies a niche below the cooling loads considered useful in the authors' earlier fuel-cell integration work (pp. 10454-10455). Its central premises are that server heat can warm seawater sufficiently for membrane distillation; that the resulting water can compensate for additional equipment and operating costs; and that efficiency and cost metrics can identify a desirable configuration. The first premise receives extensive physical development. The second depends on a much shorter set of price and lifetime assumptions. The third inherits both the upstream calculations and a chosen definition of desirability. Novelty supplies a reason to study the configuration, but cannot establish its advantage over competing heat uses or water supplies. Those alternatives appear mainly as introductory context rather than equally developed comparators.

There is real substance behind the physical proposal. Seawater carries heat away from the immersion tank and becomes the membrane module's feed; the specified 3 K approach below the dielectric's boiling temperature constrains the coupling rather than allowing arbitrary feed heating (p. 10455). The model distinguishes latent vapor transport from conduction and predicts that higher server heat raises feed temperature and water production. Table 1 reports differences below 1.5% against the selected DCMD reference calculations, while earlier work supports operation of the cooling subsystem (pp. 10459-10461). These checks make the proposal more than an appealing schematic. However, the DCMD comparison uses the same reference that supplies important module characteristics. It demonstrates consistency in selected conditions, rather than broad independent validation. The authors explicitly acknowledge that the hybrid itself has not been validated (p. 10460); that concession should govern how all subsequent results are read.

A consequential boundary assumption is the permeate inlet at 293.15 K, or 20°C, alongside seawater entering at 302.75 K (p. 10455). The scheme provides the cold stream as an inlet without demonstrating how a deployment would continuously supply it. Once-through water and recirculated water raise different supply and heat-rejection questions. Neither can simply be inferred from the pump calculation. Thus, the model establishes performance conditional on a cold-water resource, not the complete energy burden of maintaining the temperature difference. Likewise, neglecting fouling, corrosion, and salt deposition is understandable for an initial model, but these omissions bear directly on the reliability and maintenance costs needed to support a 20-year economic argument. Listing them as future experiments does not quantify their consequences.

The most serious internal difficulty concerns the metric that drives the optimization. Equation (24), labeled exergy efficiency, repeats Equation (22)'s gain output ratio: latent heat transferred through the membrane divided by server heat input (p. 10459). The displayed expression is an energy ratio and contains no explicit exergy terms. More decisively, at fixed load the model's flux calculation is independent of membrane area, so that expression increases with area. Figure 5B instead reports decreasing exergy efficiency with area and explains it through exergy destruction (p. 10464). These cannot be the same implemented quantity. A typesetting error is possible, but the paper does not supply a corrected definition that reproduces the reported surface. I therefore cannot treat the maximum exergy efficiency or its preferred small-area design as established by the published derivation.

The omission of chemical exergy creates another conceptual limit. The authors justify it by saying that stream chemical components do not change (p. 10459). Yet separating water from saline feed changes concentration and the distribution of those components. Unchanged chemical identities alone do not justify excluding the separation contribution. This does not negate the modeled heat transfer, but it weakens the interpretation of the reported quantity as a comprehensive second-law assessment of desalination. Similarly, the sustainability index is a ratio of fuel exergy to destroyed exergy. Its parallel movement with another exergy metric supplies no independent evidence about environmental impacts. The recommendation to substitute it for exergy efficiency in more complex systems requires a relationship demonstrated beyond the plotted trends of this case (p. 10465).

The economic argument has a sensible starting structure: Equation (26) compares incremental capital investment with water value minus incremental annual costs. Comparing the hybrid with otherwise identical stand-alone cooling avoids charging water production for an entire preexisting cooling service. But the numbers entering that comparison are insufficiently auditable. Equation (28) values a mass production rate using a parameter printed as 2.74 m³/h, described as Singapore's unit water cost (p. 10460). That is neither a monetary unit price nor, without conversion, compatible with a mass rate. The annual-cost equations also require time conversions that are not explicit in the displayed formulas. This matters because the 3.72-year result carries the feasibility claim.

An order-of-magnitude check exposes the stakes without pretending to repair the authors' calculation. If the intended water price were 2.74 SGD/m³, their maximum 6.13 kg/day would yield approximately 2.24 m³/year, using roughly 1000 kg/m³ and continuous operation. Its annual value would be only about 6.13 SGD. This is my conditional calculation, not a verified correction to the printed price. Table 2 lists pump equipment at 950 SGD, and the hybrid adds a permeate pump; the investment multiplier is 6.32. A few dollars of annual water value cannot readily recover that equipment increment, even before extra electricity and maintenance. A substantially different product valuation or cost interpretation would need explicit justification. The paper supplies neither clearly enough to sustain its headline payback.

The near-constant payback also deserves explanation rather than acceptance as a consequence of small scale. Across the area range, modeled water production changes fifteenfold at fixed load, while the additional pump remains present and its power is said to vary little (pp. 10463-10465). Under the stated incremental-payback structure, such a large change in the benefit with a persistent equipment increment should prompt a reconciliation. Figure 8's extremely narrow range around 3.72 years is therefore an unresolved diagnostic problem. Comparing it with an assumed 20-year lifetime cannot cure uncertainty in the cash flows that generate it. Nor do the hourly thermoeconomic cost allocations in Figure 9 independently demonstrate profitability or provide a directly comparable water price per cubic meter.

Finally, the optimization encodes preferences rather than discovering an unconditional engineering optimum. Equal 50% weights on normalized cost and efficiency are disclosed, which is a strength, but no stakeholder argument establishes those weights (p. 10463). The objectives omit a required water yield, and the selected area near 5 cm² sacrifices most of the production available at 75 cm². A decision-maker seeking useful water output could reasonably choose differently from the same modeled trends. Cooling load is also treated as selectable, although a deployment must serve its computing workload. The reported 1.1 kW and 5.13-5.19 cm² therefore describe a conditional model compromise, further weakened by the unresolved exergy definition, rather than a deployment prescription.

The authors' framing reflects their investment in an ongoing immersion-cooling research program and an engineering preference for novel integration and quantitative optimization. Their SDG framing lends importance to water production without demonstrating comparative social or environmental benefit. The disclosed university and Singapore defense-agency support identifies institutional context, not evidence of improper influence. My own emphasis on reproducible definitions and deployment boundaries may undervalue the exploratory contribution of a first model. Nevertheless, those standards become necessary when preliminary calculations are presented as economic feasibility. I would retain the paper's thermal integration as a research hypothesis and support a measured prototype with explicit cold-side accounting. I would withhold acceptance of the payback, sustainability interpretation, and recommended optimum until the definitions, units, and financial calculations are reconciled.
